# Firecrawl Fork: CRE Listing Extraction and Saving System, Full Review

**Date:** 2026-07-10
**Repo:** `agentic-assets/firecrawl` (fork of `firecrawl/firecrawl`), scope: `scripts/firecrawl-ops/cre_collector/`, `scripts/firecrawl-ops/cre_scrapers/`, `scripts/firecrawl-ops/prometheus/`, `scripts/firecrawl-ops/sql/`, `scripts/firecrawl-ops/launchd/`
**Generated by:** two independent Sonnet code-survey passes (one over `cre_collector/`, one over `cre_scrapers/` + `prometheus/` + fork-coupling), reconciled and adversarially fact-checked by an Opus verification pass that read the cited files directly. Findings below are flagged CONFIRMED where the Opus pass verified the file:line evidence itself, and softened where it found only partial support. No claim below was refuted outright, but several live-status and row-count claims are documentation assertions the verification pass could not check against the running system or database, and are labeled as such.

---

## Executive summary

This fork carries a production commercial real estate (CRE) listing pipeline that feeds the EQUIRE deal-intelligence board. It is not part of upstream Firecrawl; it is fork-owned automation layered on top of the self-hosted Firecrawl API. The live system, `scripts/firecrawl-ops/cre_collector/`, scrapes 20 major brokerage sources (CBRE, JLL, Colliers, Cushman, Savills, Newmark, Marcus & Millichap, Avison Young, Transwestern, NAI, the Buildout-hosted SVN/Lee/Franklin Street family, Matthews, SRS, Hanley, Kidder Mathews), normalizes listings to one vocabulary, and upserts into Supabase project `fhqycqubkkrdgzswccwd`, schema `credeals`, which EQUIRE reads through `v_cre_active_for_sale`, `v_cre_active_for_lease`, and related views.

The write path is unusually well defended. Status activation (the switch that lets a scrape actually flip a listing's sale/lease status) is opt-in and default-off (`cre_ingest.py:1141-1175`). Soft-delete (`--mark-missing`) is gated three separate ways and restricted to one weekly launchd tier (`cre_ingest.py:2100-2131`; `launchd/cre_run_tier.sh:250-264`). Price and detail fields use COALESCE-keep semantics so a transient scrape miss never blanks good data (`cre_ingest.py:1348-1370`). This is careful, defensive engineering for a system whose failure mode is corrupting a live investor-facing board.

Set against that, three things should get the founder's attention. First, per the system's own documentation, three of its four scheduled launchd tiers (enrich, daily, weekly) were last reported failing (`rc:1`) as of the most recent status snapshot, with no in-repo root cause; this report treats that as a documented claim, not a live-verified fact, but it is worth checking `cre_status.sh` before relying on board freshness. Second, `cre_ingest.py` is a 2,180-line single-file monolith that assembles SQL as text and is tested mostly through dry-run string assertions rather than against a real database engine. Third, and most decision-relevant: fact-checking this review surfaced a second, apparently independent system (referred to in source material as "GetCREdata" / Repo B) that writes into the same Supabase project and schema, including a table this repo's own documentation says should still be empty (`cre_listing_om_facts`, reported by the other repo's docs at 398,040 rows) and a conflict-key definition that does not match this repo's schema. Neither repo's code or docs mentions the other by name. That is an unsynchronized, undocumented shared-write situation on production data and is the single highest-priority item in this review.

Separately, a large legacy Python tree (`cre_scrapers/`, `cre_pipeline.py`) and a frozen reference archive (`prometheus/`) sit in the repo unscheduled and untested, adding real maintenance surface (duplicated normalization logic, ~300k lines of archived JSON) without runtime footprint.

---

## What it is and what it does (plain English)

Picture a machine that spends the day visiting the websites of large commercial real estate brokerages (CBRE, JLL, Colliers, and so on), reads every property listing it can find, figures out the price, square footage, cap rate, address, and broker contact for each one, and files it away in one shared database. That database is what powers the EQUIRE product's "browse live listings" and "search comparable properties" features. This system is that machine.

It runs on a schedule (not on demand) from a single Mac mini in the office, not in the cloud. It does not scrape brokerage sites directly; it routes every request through this fork's own self-hosted copy of Firecrawl running locally, which handles the actual page-rendering and anti-bot evasion. Once a page comes back, source-specific code translates that brokerage's page layout into one common listing format, and a separate Python step writes that into Postgres.

The system is deliberately cautious about touching the "front door" of the product. Even when it successfully determines a listing has sold or is off the market, by default it does not flip that status live, because a bad scrape could otherwise take a listing off the board incorrectly. That safety switch has to be turned on explicitly, and even then several more checks have to pass first.

There is also an older, abandoned version of this idea (`cre_scrapers/`, a Python package with its own per-broker scrapers) sitting in the same repository. It is not on any schedule and both the code's own documentation and this review confirm it does not affect the live board. It exists as leftover exploration, not as a second production path.

---

## Architecture and data flow

**Language split.** Three layers, three languages, one shared destination.

1. **TypeScript collector** (Node via `tsx`): `collect.ts` is the orchestrator, with a `runSource` switch handling all 20 source keys (`cre_collector/collect.ts:62-241`). Source keys live in one tuple (`cre_collector/types.ts:11-33`), and adapter code for each broker lives in `cre_collector/sources/*.ts` (19 files covering 20 keys, since SVN, Lee & Associates, and Franklin Street all route through a shared `buildout.ts` adapter for their common Buildout-hosted platform). Its only real dependency is `@mendable/firecrawl-js` plus `cheerio` (`cre_collector/package.json`).
2. **Python ingest/monitor/enrich layer** (stdlib only, shells out to `psql`): `cre_ingest.py` (2,180 lines, the upsert engine), `cre_monitor.py` (1,187 lines, observe-only change tracking), `cre_gate.py` (489 lines, coverage gate), `cre_enrich.py` (551 lines, Tier-B queue worker), plus `cre_parse.py`/`cre_geo.py` as Python mirrors of the TypeScript parsing/geo logic.
3. **Bash operations layer**: `cre_daily_update.sh`, `launchd/cre_run_tier.sh` (the portable, lock-protected tier dispatcher), `launchd/install_launchd.sh` (renders per-machine plists), `cre_status.sh` (read-only heartbeat), `cre_setup.sh`.

**Request path.** Broker site to local self-hosted Firecrawl API at `http://localhost:3002` (`cre_collector/lib/config.ts:4`), via the `firecrawl-js` SDK with a 3-attempt retry loop (`cre_collector/lib/scrape.ts:7-32`), using stealth proxy mode for Cloudflare-protected sites and requesting markdown/links/images/rawHtml/attributes formats. Each source adapter then maps the raw payload into the shared listing vocabulary.

**Three run modes share this same collector, diverging after collection:**

- **Full collect to production ingest.** `collect.ts` writes one JSON artifact per run (`mode: full|monitor|enrich`, plus `sources[]`, `listings[]`, `brokers[]`) under `out/` (`collect.ts:216-240`). `cre_ingest.py` reads the artifact, normalizes each row (`to_row()`), folds sale and lease passes for the same property into `transaction_type = sale_or_lease` (`merge_rows()`), `COPY`s into a temp staging table, and upserts into `credeals.cre_listings` keyed on `(brokerage_id, external_id)`, refreshing child tables (contacts, documents, images), all inside one `psql` transaction with `ON_ERROR_STOP=1`.
- **Monitor (observe-only).** A cheap enumeration-only collect feeds `cre_monitor.py`, which writes to the append-only "007" change-tracking tables (`cre_source_index`, `cre_listing_events`) and enqueues new/changed listings into `cre_enrichment_queue`. This path never writes to `cre_listings` itself.
- **Enrich (Tier-B).** `cre_enrich.py` claims a batch from `cre_enrichment_queue`, runs `collect.ts --enrich-input` for a targeted detail-page render on just those URLs, and re-ingests the results additively (never with `--mark-missing` or `--activate-status`), then deletes the completed queue rows.

EQUIRE reads the result exclusively through Postgres views (`v_cre_active_for_sale`, `v_cre_active_for_lease`, `v_cre_listings_full`, `v_cre_market_summary`, `v_cre_recent_changes`) and a `search_cre_listings(...)` function, also exposed through the EQUIRE MCP server's `get_listing`/`search_listings` tools.

**A caveat worth flagging on this section.** The fact-check pass corrected one claim in the source survey: the 20 source keys are described in one place as "one canonical tuple consumed by both `collect.ts` and the ingest mapping." In fact there are two independent, manually duplicated definitions of that same 20-key list: the TypeScript `SOURCE_KEYS` tuple (`cre_collector/types.ts:11-32`), whose own comment scopes it only to `collect.ts` and `lib/enrich.ts`, and a separate Python dictionary, `SOURCE_TO_BROKERAGE` (`cre_ingest.py:74-93`). Python cannot import the TypeScript constant, so today the two lists happen to match, but nothing enforces that they stay in sync if a source is ever added or renamed. This is a real change-coupling risk, addressed further under Weaknesses.

## Storage schema

**Target:** Supabase project `fhqycqubkkrdgzswccwd` ("supabase-agentic-assets-v2"), schema `credeals` (`sql/002_cre_listings.sql:4`). The ingest process talks to Postgres by shelling out to `psql` directly, no ORM or driver (`cre_ingest.py` `find_psql()` and `subprocess.run([psql, db_url, "-q", "-v", "ON_ERROR_STOP=1", "-f", sql_path])`, roughly `cre_ingest.py:2167-2175`).

**Core tables (sql/001-006):** `cre_brokerages`, `cre_listings` (UUID primary key, `status` constrained to `active/inactive/sold/leased/expired/withdrawn`, `sql/002:29-31`), plus child tables `cre_listing_contacts`, `cre_listing_documents`, `cre_listing_images`, and operational tables `cre_scrape_jobs`, `cre_scrape_log`.

**Change-tracking layer, "007" (`sql/007`):** `cre_listing_events` (append-only ledger, cascades from the parent listing), `cre_source_index`, `cre_enrichment_queue`, `cre_source_baseline`. These back the observe-only monitor path described above.

**History/archive layer, "009" (`sql/009`):** `cre_listing_price_history`, `cre_listing_contacts_archive`, `cre_listing_documents_archive`. Archive tables carry no foreign keys, so they survive even a hard delete of the parent listing, intentionally, for auditability.

**Phase-2 tables, "011-014" (`sql/011` through `sql/014`), confirmed applied to production:** `cre_listing_media`, `cre_listing_links` (each with an `*_archive` mirror), institutional and geo scalar columns plus `extra_facts` jsonb on `cre_listings`, a `license` column on `cre_listing_contacts`, `cre_listing_om_facts` (with archive), and `cre_zip_cbsa_crosswalk` (loaded with 33,791 rows, 24,734 carrying a resolved CBSA). Per this fork's own documentation as of its most recent update, `cre_listing_om_facts`, `cre_listing_media`, and `cre_listing_links` were expected to remain **empty**, since OM-document parsing and media capture are still feature-gated off.

**That expectation does not hold up.** Fact-checking this review against a second CRE system present on the same Supabase project (referred to in source material as "GetCREdata," not part of this fork, not mentioned anywhere in this repo's code or docs) found that system's own documentation reports 398,040 rows already present in `credeals.cre_listing_om_facts`, dated after this repo's "remains EMPTY" claim. Neither figure was queried live against the database for this report; both are documentation assertions, and they directly contradict each other. What can be said with confidence: a second, independent pipeline is writing into a table this fork's operators believe is inert, using a Postgres REST client (`supabase-py`) rather than this fork's direct `psql` path, and using a 5-column `on_conflict` key (`listing_id, fact_group, fact_key, source_doc_url, parser_version`) against a table whose actual unique index in this repo's schema has only 4 columns (`listing_id, fact_group, fact_key, source_doc_url`, `sql/013_cre_listing_om_facts.sql:69`, `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`). That other system's own README describes the 4-column index correctly, so its write path is internally inconsistent with its own documentation as well as with this repo's schema, and any 5-column conflict clause would fail against the actual index unless a second, undocumented index also exists. This is covered further under Risks; it should not be treated as resolved by this report.

**Consumer views.** All `v_cre_*` views run with `security_invoker = true` and filter to `deleted_at IS NULL AND status IN ('active', 'under_contract', 'pending')` (`sql/005_cre_views.sql:126,162-170,206-214,245,379`), reflecting an already-widened status filter beyond the historical "active only" definition.

**File outputs (gitignored, not database):** per-run JSON artifacts and log/verdict markers under `out/daily/`, `out/monitor/`, `out/enrich/`, and per-source detail caches under `out/cache/`.

## How it runs today (operational reality)

The pipeline runs on the Mac mini (`cayman-mac-mini`) via `launchd`, not in the cloud. Four scheduled tiers are dispatched through one script, `launchd/cre_run_tier.sh`, which serializes all of them behind a single atomic `mkdir`-based lock (`out/daily/.cre.lock`) with PID-based stale-lock recovery. If one tier is already running, a competing tier exits cleanly rather than colliding.

Per this fork's most recent status documentation:

| Tier | Cadence | Purpose | Last reported run status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monitor | 2x/day, 06:10 and 18:10 | observe-only change detection, enqueues enrichment work | OK (`rc:0`) |
| Enrich | every 4 hours | drains `cre_enrichment_queue`, targeted re-scrape and additive re-ingest | reported FAILED (`rc:1`) |
| Daily | 06:30 | full-refresh ingest (role now described as "retired," kept for rollback) | reported FAILED (`rc:1`) |
| Weekly | Sunday 03:00 | additive backstop; the only tier permitted to soft-delete, and only under `CRE_WEEKLY_MARK_MISSING=1` | reported FAILED (`rc:1`) |

This report did not independently query `launchd` or the live logs to confirm these statuses; it is relaying what this repository's own documentation states as of its last update. The practical implication, if accurate, is that the enrichment queue and the freshness backstop (which is the only mechanism that can soft-delete stale listings) have not been running successfully, and nothing short of manually running `cre_status.sh` surfaces that: there is no alerting layer.

The pipeline hard-depends on the local self-hosted Firecrawl stack answering at `http://localhost:3002`; `cre_daily_update.sh:86-92` runs a health-check gate that aborts the run if the stack is down. Production credentials load from an EQUIRE environment file (`CRE_ENV_FILE`, production path `~/.config/cre/equire.env`), which supplies `POSTGRES_URL_NON_POOLING` or `POSTGRES_URL` (`cre_ingest.py:1855-1886`). The code takes care to print only the resolved file path at run time, never the URL value itself (`cre_ingest.py:2166`). Default fallback paths for that env file, when `CRE_ENV_FILE` is unset, point at `~/Documents` (`cre_ingest.py:62-65`); a misconfigured environment falls through to those defaults silently rather than failing loudly.

The most recent code change to the collector itself, per git history, predates the most recent documentation updates by roughly two weeks, a pattern that recurs throughout this subsystem's ~30-plus markdown status files.

## Strengths

- **Status activation is opt-in and default-off.** `_status_activation_enabled()` and `apply_status_activation_gate()` (`cre_ingest.py:1141-1175`) mean routine ingests cannot silently flip a listing's live sale/lease status; when the feature is off, incoming statuses are discarded before the upsert, and `COALESCE(NULL, 'active')` keeps existing rows as-is.
- **Soft-delete is defense-in-depth, not a single check.** `--mark-missing` requires, per brokerage, an error-free pass, a minimum row floor, and count-aware coverage across any folded source group (`cre_ingest.py:2100-2131`), on top of which `cre_gate.py --strict` can auto-downgrade the entire daily run to additive-only if it detects a coverage problem (`cre_daily_update.sh:112-117`), and even then, only the weekly tier may execute a soft-delete, and only with an explicit environment flag set (`launchd/cre_run_tier.sh:250-264`).
- **Upserts are conservative by default.** Price, cap rate, and similar numeric fields use `COALESCE(EXCLUDED.x, t.x)` (`cre_ingest.py:1348-1370`), so a page that fails to parse a field on one run does not blank out a previously good value, and child rows (contacts, documents, images) are preserved rather than wiped when a detail scrape errors (`cre_ingest.py:1519-1528`).
- **Monitor is provably observe-only.** `coverage_decision()` (`cre_monitor.py:85-108`) refuses to treat a source as "disappeared" if that pass errored or was truncated, and this cannot be overridden even by a `--force-disappear` flag, by explicit code comment and logic order.
- **An optional circuit breaker exists for mass reclassification.** `CRE_STATUS_FLIP_MAX_FRACTION` (`cre_ingest.py:1114-1138`, enforced via a `RAISE EXCEPTION` guard at `1394-1444`) aborts the entire transaction if a single ingest run would reclassify more than a configured fraction of a source's active inventory, protecting against a bad scrape mass-flipping listings.
- **SQL construction is injection-hardened.** `standard_conforming_strings` is pinned before any literal or COPY payload is emitted (`cre_ingest.py:1190`), string literals are quote-doubled, and the database URL is passed as an argv value, never interpolated into printed output or logs.
- **Test coverage is substantial for this kind of pipeline.** Roughly 1,274 distinct pytest functions plus a parallel TypeScript unit-test suite, including golden-vector parity tests that lock the Python parsing mirror (`cre_parse.py`) to the TypeScript source of truth (`lib/parse.ts`), and a test that checks the monitor/gate/ingest source-key enumeration stays consistent.
- **The whole system is additive-by-construction.** DDL-optional blocks guarded by `to_regclass`/`information_schema` checks let the same ingest code run safely both before and after a schema migration, and append-only history/archive tables provide durable auditability independent of the live table state.

---

## Weaknesses and technical debt

- **`cre_ingest.py` is a 2,180-line monolith.** It assembles one large SQL script as a Python string and executes it in a single `psql` call; the core upsert, mark-missing, and history logic (`cre_ingest.py:1178-1843`) is testable mainly through dry-run text assertions rather than against a real database engine, which limits how much confidence the test suite alone can provide about correctness at the SQL level.
- **Live run health is degraded, by the system's own reporting.** Enrich, daily, and weekly tiers were last reported failing (`rc:1`), with no root cause captured anywhere in-repo. This is a documentation claim this report could not verify against the live system, but if accurate, it means the enrichment queue and the only soft-delete backstop are not currently functioning, silently.
- **Hardcoded fallback credential paths point at `~/Documents`** (`cre_ingest.py:62-65`). Portability depends entirely on `CRE_ENV_FILE` being set correctly; a missing or misconfigured environment variable falls through quietly instead of failing loudly at startup.
- **Tight coupling to one host and one repo checkout.** The pipeline cannot run unless the fork's local Firecrawl stack answers at `localhost:3002` (`lib/config.ts:4`; `cre_daily_update.sh:86-92` references the fork directory directly for its health check), binding collection to both this specific checkout and the single Mac mini.
- **Several adapters are fragile against anti-bot defenses.** Heavy reliance on stealth-proxy retries for Cloudflare-protected sources (for example `sources/cbre.ts:141`, `sources/colliers-main.ts`); Savills' US commercial-sale feed is structurally capped near zero rows because no public feed exists for it (`sources/savills.ts:225-278,533-537`); Newmark's Algolia-backed search caps at 1,000 hits; OM (offering memorandum) PDF fetches are blocked locally by anti-bot measures. All of this depends on a single residential IP, which is itself a risk (see Risks).
- **The Firecrawl SDK is called through untyped `as any` casts** (`lib/scrape.ts:16-21,38-66`), so a breaking change in the SDK's response shape would only surface at runtime, not at compile time.
- **Board freshness has a structural gap by design.** Because status activation stays off by default, sold or leased listings remain marked "active" until a `--mark-missing` sweep runs, and that sweep is itself gated and currently reported as failing on its only scheduled carrier (the weekly tier).
- **Documentation sprawl invites drift.** Roughly 30 dated handoff/status markdown files live under `cre_collector/` alone, several of which exist purely to redirect an agent away from legacy code; the repo's own `START_HERE.md` warns that any live count it cites can go stale within hours. The last collector code change and the most recent documentation update are roughly two weeks apart, and this pattern (docs describing a different step count or status than the code implements) recurs; see the GetCREdata example below, where one repo's README claims a "25-step" pipeline, its own CLAUDE.md claims "26-step," and the actual code runs 30 steps (`run.py:92`).
- **Parallel legacy systems remain present** (`cre_scrapers/`, `cre_pipeline.py`, `cbre_scrape.py`) despite explicit "do not use" documentation, creating ongoing ambiguity about which code path an unfamiliar contributor or agent should edit.
- **Wiring a new source requires touching four or more places by hand**, with nothing enforcing consistency between them: `collect.ts`, `cre_ingest.py`'s `SOURCE_TO_BROKERAGE`, `lib/enrich.ts`, and the seed data in `sql/001`. A partial wiring silently mis-keys rows or breaks coverage-fold logic.
- **The 20-source-key list is duplicated, not shared**, as corrected in the Architecture section above: a TypeScript tuple and a Python dictionary that happen to agree today with nothing enforcing that they continue to.

---

## Risks

- **Single point of failure.** All collection and ingest runs on one Mac mini against one local Docker stack. If OrbStack, the machine, or the local API is down, the entire pipeline halts with no cloud fallback; a cloud-hosting option has been documented as a decision aid but not implemented.
- **Silent degradation.** If three of four scheduled tiers are indeed failing as documented, that failure surfaces only if someone runs `cre_status.sh` manually; there is no alerting path, so board staleness and a stalled enrichment queue could persist unnoticed.
- **Anti-bot and IP-block exposure.** Aggressive multi-source scraping from a single residential IP risks a Cloudflare or rate-limit block that could cascade across sources; several adapters (Savills, OM PDF fetches) already run in a degraded state.
- **Board correctness while status activation stays off.** Sold or leased inventory can persist as "active" on the live board until a mark-missing sweep runs, and that sweep's only scheduled carrier is reported as currently failing.
- **Credential exposure surface.** The production `POSTGRES_URL` (a direct, non-pooling Postgres connection that bypasses row-level security) lives in a local environment file (`~/.config/cre/equire.env`) on one machine; a leak of that file grants full write access to the EQUIRE `credeals` schema.
- **Scraping/ToS exposure.** Bulk collection of brokerage listing data at this scale is inherently sensitive from a terms-of-service standpoint and could draw blocking or a complaint from a source site.
- **Change-coupling risk on new sources.** Because source wiring is spread across four-plus files with no automated cross-check, a partially wired source can mis-key rows or silently break coverage calculations that gate mark-missing.
- **Undocumented shared-write on the same production schema.** This is the most consequential finding from fact-checking this review. A second CRE data system (referred to in source material as "GetCREdata"), not part of this repository and never mentioned in this fork's code or docs, writes into the same Supabase project (`fhqycqubkkrdgzswccwd`) and the same `credeals` schema:
  - It reads `credeals.cre_zip_cbsa_crosswalk`, the geo table this fork created via `sql/014_cre_geo_crosswalk.sql`.
  - It writes into `credeals.cre_listing_om_facts` using a Supabase REST client (`supabase-py`) with a service-role key, an entirely different write path than this fork's direct `psql` approach.
  - Its documented row count for that table (398,040, reported later) directly contradicts this fork's documentation, which states the table "remains EMPTY" (reported earlier). Neither figure was verified live for this report.
  - Its `on_conflict` clause for that table uses 5 columns (including `parser_version`), which does not match this fork's actual 4-column unique index (`sql/013:69`), and does not even match that other system's own README, which correctly describes the 4-column index. That write path, as documented, appears internally inconsistent and would be expected to error against this fork's real schema unless an undocumented second index exists.
  - Because neither system is aware of the other, there is no coordination on the shared upsert key, status lifecycle, or mark-missing semantics; this is the highest-risk consolidation seam identified in this review, and it warrants a direct conversation with whoever owns "GetCREdata" before any further schema changes are made to `credeals` from either side.
- **Documentation-vs-reality drift generally.** Given the two contradictions found above (this repo's own commit-date-vs-doc-date gap, and the cross-repo OM-facts contradiction), any status figure or row count sourced from a markdown file in either repository should be treated as provisional until confirmed against the live system.

---

## What is legacy vs live

**Live, production, scheduled:** `scripts/firecrawl-ops/cre_collector/` in its entirety, comprising the TypeScript collector (`collect.ts`, `types.ts`, `lib/`, `sources/*.ts`), the Python ingest/monitor/gate/enrich scripts, and the `launchd/` tier dispatcher. This is confirmed by this repo's own routing documentation, which explicitly marks `cre_collector` ACTIVE and `cre_scrapers` STALE, and by the absence of any scheduling reference (cron, launchd plist, or package script) to the legacy tree.

**Legacy, unscheduled, zero test coverage:** `scripts/firecrawl-ops/cre_scrapers/` (a parallel Python package: `base.py`'s `BaseScraper`, per-broker `brokers/<slug>/scraper.py` files for 10 configured slugs, of which only three, CBRE, Colliers, and NAI Global, have real logic beyond a generic stub) and the top-level `cre_pipeline.py` orchestrator (`CREScrapingPipeline`, ~432 lines). A repo-wide search found no test file anywhere that references either `cre_scrapers` or `cre_pipeline`. This code still runs if invoked directly and can still write to Supabase via a legacy REST path using `SUPABASE_URL`/`SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY`, so it is not inert, only unscheduled; an unfamiliar contributor asked to "fix the CRE scraper" could plausibly resurrect it and write through a path its own documentation warns must never touch the 007 change-tracking tables.

**Reference-only, frozen:** `scripts/firecrawl-ops/prometheus/`, explicitly documented as "reference material, do not modify," containing the original cloud-based CBRE API-discovery script that `cre_collector`'s CBRE adapter was adapted from, plus an 11 MB, roughly 300,000-line static `data.json` snapshot dated to a single point in time. It is read only for manual inspection and consumed by no pipeline.

**Real, non-hypothetical duplication that persists despite the legacy label:** `cre_scrapers/normalizer.py` independently reimplements price, square footage, state, cap-rate, and phone-number normalization in Python (`normalizer.py:114-330`), parallel to the same job done in TypeScript by the live `lib/parse.ts` and `lib/geo.ts`. Nothing keeps a business-rule fix made in one from being missed in the other; because the legacy copy has no scheduled run and no tests, a rule fixed there would never surface as broken, and a rule fixed only in the live path would leave the legacy path wrong indefinitely, which matters only if the legacy path is ever run again, but the file otherwise sits as an unmonitored second copy of core parsing logic.

**Fork-coupling in general.** Roughly 343 of the repository's 2,479 tracked files (about 14 percent) live under `scripts/firecrawl-ops/`, against 1,317 files under `apps/` (upstream Firecrawl product code). This fork syncs from `firecrawl/firecrawl:main` roughly every one to two weeks, with individual syncs touching 50 to 180 files and thousands of changed lines (one recent sync: 176 files, +11,398/-4,780 lines). A hand-maintained `PROTECTED_PATHS` allowlist in `sync_upstream_main.sh:41-47` (covering `.agents`, `docs/firecrawl-ops`, `scripts/firecrawl-ops`, `LOCAL_DEVELOPMENT_GUIDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`) is what keeps upstream merges from clobbering this fork-owned CRE system; nothing automatically verifies that allowlist stays exhaustive as new fork-owned files are added outside those five entries. The collector's actual scraping and ingest logic, by contrast, is only loosely coupled to this fork: it reads `FIRECRAWL_API_URL`/`FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` from the environment and would run against any Firecrawl endpoint, self-hosted or cloud; the only hard dependency on this specific repository is the convenience tooling (`cre_setup.sh`, `cre_status.sh`) that resolves the fork's directory to run Docker Compose health checks.

---
